posts.caption: The farrier comes every six weeks, always on a Tuesday, always at 7:30, always with the same radio station playing in his truck. Big Red knows the sound of that truck from the far end of the pasture. By the time he's got his apron on, she's already planted all four feet like fence posts. He talks to her the whole time, sweet as anything, and she lets him have the fronts. The hinds are a negotiation. Last time it took a bucket of grain, two of us, and most of his patience. He still calls her his favorite. I think he means it.
posts.first: My first horse would only let the farrier pick up his feet if I sang. Not hummed. Sang. For eleven years I stood in that barn aisle doing every hymn I knew from memory while a grown man trimmed hooves and pretended not to hear me.

posts.caption: I hung a little bucket of apple treats on the fence post by the gate so I'd have something on hand during training. The pony and I were working on standing still while I opened the gate. Simple. Three days in, he'd mastered standing still. He stands still by that fence post most of the afternoon now. He stands still when I walk past it. He stands still when the mail carrier walks past it. Yesterday I found him standing perfectly still with his nose an inch from the bucket and his eyes closed, like he was praying. I moved the bucket.
posts.first: I once tried keeping treats in my jacket pocket instead of a bucket. Within a week my pony could tell which jacket I was wearing from across the arena. He ignored the barn coat completely and followed the blue one around like a shadow. I wear the barn coat now.

Text at the top reads: She said the treats are for good behavior. Text at the bottom reads: So I've been behaving near the treats.

posts.quote: My mare pinned her ears at the new gelding for three weeks. Today he left for one trail ride and she screamed the whole hour.
posts.first: My old mare hated every horse she ever shared a fence with, and loved each one the minute it left. When her pasture buddy moved to a new home, she stood at that corner of the fence for two days. I hung a mirror in her stall. She pinned her ears at it.

posts.caption: Our old lesson horse officially retired the spring he turned twenty-eight. We gave him the best stall, the one with the window, and a sign on the door that says he's done working. Nobody told him. Saturday mornings he's at the arena gate by nine, same as he's been for twenty years. Last month a woman came out for her first lesson in decades, nervous as a cat in a borrowed helmet. The instructor looked at the gate, then at me. I went and got his bridle. He stood for the mounting block like a gentleman. Retirement can wait.
posts.first: My grandfather retired from the feed mill at sixty-five and drove past it every morning for another ten years. He said he was checking on the place. Nobody ever asked him to. I think about him every Saturday when I see that old gray waiting by the gate.

posts.caption: Every horse I've ever owned has been led, saddled, and mounted from the left, because that's how it's done. This mare took the rule personally. Walk up on her left and she's a dream, lowering her head for the halter like a duchess. Walk up on her right and she looks at you like you've tracked mud across her carpet. Our new barn help made that mistake on day one, coming up on the right with a bottle of fly spray. She swung her whole back end around and stood facing the wall for ten minutes. He brings her carrots now. From the left.
posts.first: When I was learning to ride, my instructor had me lead her old gelding from the right side for a whole week so he wouldn't get set in his ways. He tolerated it. Then on Friday he walked me straight into the manure pile. Lesson learned, apparently by both of us.

Text at the top reads: I'm not difficult. I just have a left side and a wrong side.

posts.quote: I don't spook at the tractor, the dogs, or the hay delivery. I spook at the one spot in the arena where nothing has ever happened. Something will. I can feel it.
posts.caption: There's a spot in the far corner of our indoor arena, about six feet from the kickboard, where there is nothing. No mirror, no door, no gap in the wall. I've checked. I've walked it on foot and kicked the dirt around. The mare still gives it a full sideways hop every time we pass. Meanwhile, last week the hay guy backed his truck in with a flapping tarp and she didn't twitch. She just walked over to see if he'd brought anything for her. We've started calling it the haunted corner. She has not disagreed.
posts.first: My trainer once rode my mare past that corner for half an hour straight to prove there was nothing there. She held steady on every single pass. The second I climbed back on, the mare looked at the corner, looked back at me, and hopped right on cue.
